problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/fa7f40460a8834c73c61575aef821157e1aff7dace359752fd98593271812c10.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,y({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4),\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $2$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,y({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4),\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the left and right sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/1f00f0e9fa8148ca3cf161322c926ea9fc16a4467991063cbdcb4f293254674d.png)

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=2$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,y({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4),\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =2({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{1} & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,z)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{D}({r}^{2}+4)\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}r({r}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}({r}^{3}+4r)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}({r}^{3}+4r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}+2{r}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\pi (\frac{1}{4}+2) \\  & =9\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,0,z)=⟨0,\,0({x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4),\,0⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =9\pi +0 \\  & =9\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨0,y(x2+z2+4),0⟩ and the surface S defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height 2 whose base is a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of F through S.

a
3π2
b
4π
c

Correct
EXPLANATION

If S is an oriented surface with unit normal vector n, and F is continuous vector field, then the flux of F across S measured with respect to n is given by ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS.

Notice that only the y-component of F=⟨0,y(x2+z2+4),0⟩ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of S is parallel to the y-axis, the flux of F through S will be non-zero only at the left and right sides.


Let's consider the flux of F through these two sides.

  • Let S1 denote the right surface. On this surface, we have y=2 for x2+z2≤1. The outward-pointing unit normal vector to S1 is n1=⟨0,1,0⟩. Using the fact that y=2 on S1, we have F⋅n1=⟨0,y(x2+z2+4),0⟩⋅⟨0,1,0⟩=⟨0,2(x2+z2+4),0⟩⋅⟨0,1,0⟩=2(x2+z2+4). Therefore, the flux of F across S1 is given by ∬S1F⋅dS1=∬S1F⋅n1dS=∬S12(x2+z2+4)dS=2∬D(x2+z2+4)dA. Applying a change of variables (x,z)→(r,θ),dA=rdrdθ, we have 2∬D(x2+z2+4)dA=2∬D(r2+4)⋅rdrdθ=2∫02π∫01r(r2+4)drdθ=2∫02π∫01(r3+4r)drdθ=2∫02πdθ∫01(r3+4r)dr=2⋅2π⋅[14r4+2r2]01=4π(14+2)=9π.

  • Let S2 denote the left surface. On this surface, we have y=0 for x2+z2≤1. Therefore, for everywhere on S2, we have F(x,0,z)=⟨0,0(x2+z2+4),0⟩=⟨0,0,0⟩. Therefore, ∬S2F⋅ndS=∬S20⋅ndS=∬S20dS=0.

Finally, ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬S1F⋅ndS+∬S2F⋅ndS=9π+0=9π.
